idiom_name: mockito-scala mock[T]/spy, or a subclass of an open class
implementation_notes: On the JVM the dominant route is Mockito (mockito-scala), which subclasses or instruments the class under test and lets doReturn(...).when(sut).now() replace only the boundary; the hand-written route is a plain subclass - Scala 2 leaves non-final classes open, while Scala 3 requires open or the scala.language.adhocExtensions opt-in, whose documentation explicitly frames ad-hoc extension as something to reach for in tests with mocks. Scala's mandatory override keyword removes Java's silent-shadowing failure mode, and case classes are final, so value types need a trait plus a fake instead of a subclass.
code_sketch:
class TimeDisplayTss extends TimeDisplay {     // Scala 3: TimeDisplay must be open
  private var fixed: Instant = _
  override protected def now(): Instant = fixed
  def setNow(t: Instant): Unit = fixed = t     // control point
}

val sut = spy(new TimeDisplay()); doReturn(fixed).when(sut).now()   // mockito-scala
pitfalls: Extending a non-open class in another file in Scala 3 is a feature warning gated behind scala.language.adhocExtensions; with -Xfatal-warnings (common in CI) the test fails to compile.
case classes and final classes cannot be subclassed and sealed/enum hierarchies are closed - none of them can host a test seam.
mockito-scala's mock[T] is a macro that needs T to be concrete at the call site: wrapping it in a non-inline helper loses by-name/vararg metadata and stubs then fail to match at runtime.
